unit.sep: Construct/check models,identify patterns,conserve charge/atoms and distinguish evidence from representation.
unit.careers: Illustrative chemical analysis,materials science and teaching roles;no actual chemical handling.
unit.focus: Classification of the first twenty elements of the periodic table; Electron configuration of atoms of elements; Ion formation; Valency and oxidation number; Chemical formulae of common compounds; Chemical equations
unit.phenomenon: A fictional periodic-table poster claims every first20 element forms a simple ion and changes chemical subscripts to balance reactions.
unit.supportingPhenomena: First20reference,shell/charge models,ion drawings,substance-chart audit and fixed chemical skeletons.
unit.drivingQuestion: How can atomic structure explain periodic patterns and help us check chemical formulae and equations?
unit.content: Classification of the first twenty elements of the periodic table; Electron configuration of atoms of elements; Ion formation; Valency and oxidation number; Chemical formulae of common compounds; Chemical equations
unit.coreCompetencies:
Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: as the learner sorts and arranges the first twenty elements of the periodic table according to their similarities.
Creativity and Imagination: as the learner models the electron configuration of any five elements of the periodic table using locally available materials.
unit.values:
Respect: as the learner recognises and respects the input of every group member as they discuss how to determine the valency and oxidation numbers of elements and radicals.
Unity: as the learner takes turns in playing roles when drawing dot (.) and cross (x) diagrams to illustrate ion formation for atoms of elements of the periodic table.
Responsibility: as the learner uses digital devices appropriately to watch simulations and animations on ion formation.
unit.pcis:
Life skills (Problem solving skills): as the learner arranges the first twenty elements of the periodic table into groups and periods.
Financial literacy: as the learner uses locally available materials as a way of minimising the expenses when modelling the electron configuration of any five elements of the periodic table.
keyInquiryQuestions: How are elements arranged in the periodic table?
unit.teacherConfirmationRequired: Confirm resources/access/pacing and actual project/digital actions;retain stated model/energy/charge limits.

assessment.instructions: Independent40minute written assessment using onlyPT15 and these prompts. Timing:4minutes read,8Section1,10Section2,12Sections3–4,6Section5/check/submit. No teacher answer hints or teaching-card keys. Draw actual requested diagrams and show charge/atom checks. This final does not certify project/digital performance.

sections.title: 1. Atomic structure and periodic classification
sections.prompt: Using PT15,for A,B,C identify the element and give p,n,e,shell population,group and period. Explain why He belongs in group18 although its first shell has2electrons.
sections.exemplar: A Mg:p12,n12,e12;2,8,2;group2,period3. B F:p9,n10,e9;2,7;group17,period2. C Ar:p18,n22,e18;2,8,8;group18,period3. He has a complete first shell2 and noble-gas properties,not an ordinary group2 pattern.

sections.title: 2. Transfer,stability and electron affinity
sections.prompt: Draw before/after dot/cross outer-electron diagrams for the compound of A and B,showing transfer,count,brackets,charges and any omitted inner shells. Give its formula and explain why C is relatively unreactive. Compare fictional P/Q attachment energies using the given convention;explain one conclusion these energies cannot establish.
sections.exemplar: Mg transfers2electrons,one to each of twoF atoms. Mg2+ has2,8;eachF−has2,8 and outer7dots+1cross;brackets2+/−and legend needed,inner shells may be omitted with note. Ratio1:2 givesMgF2. Ar has a closed outer shell and is relatively unreactive. P releases25>Q5units,but these fictional atom records do not prove a compound forms or identify real elements.

sections.title: 3. Formulae and oxidation numbers
sections.prompt: Use PT15 ions to write calcium nitrate and ammonium phosphate formulae with charge totals. Explain parentheses. Give oxidation numbers ofCa/O inCaO andO in elementalO2;distinguish oxidation number from unsigned valency.
sections.exemplar: Ca(NO3)2:+2+2(−1)=0;(NH4)3PO4:3(+1)−3=0;parentheses multiply intact polyatomic groups. CaO:Ca+2,O−2;O2:O0. Valency is an unsigned combining capacity here,not a signed oxidation number.

sections.title: 4. Conservation in equations
sections.prompt: Balance both PT15 skeletons using smallest positive whole-number coefficients and give full atom counts on each side. Explain why changing a product subscript is not balancing.
sections.exemplar: 2Ca+O2→2CaO:Ca2,O2 each side.4NH3+3O2→2N2+6H2O:N4,H12,O6 each side. Coefficients multiply whole formulae;subscript changes alter substance identity.

sections.title: 5. Why structure matters
sections.prompt: Explain two ways atomic structure supports periodic classification and chemical-formula reasoning,using examples from this record. State a precise shell/ion-model limit and whether this written task establishes actual project or animation performance.
sections.exemplar: Mg2,8,2 has3occupied shells/period3 and2outer electrons/group2;loss2matchesMg2+and its1:2fluoride charge ratio. Shell patterns help organise families but do not force every element into a simple ion or prove reaction energetics. Written work does not establish actual five-model/chart construction or digital viewing.
